newsitem.title: USA: Tight US job mart may not push wages-Cleveland Fed.
newsitem.headline: Tight US job mart may not push wages-Cleveland Fed.

text.p: The low U.S. unemployment rate reflects tight labor markets but it is still unclear whether it is inflationary, a senior official at the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland said on Wednesday.

"The current unemployment rate is giving a measure of tighteness in the labor market, but it is unclear whether to correlate that tighteness with wage changes," senior vice president and director of research Mark Sniderman told Reuters.

The U.S. unemployment rate stood at 5.2 percent or below in August-October. One school of economists say 5.75 percent is the maximum non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU). They say an unemployment rate that steadily remains below the natural rate will ultimately result in higher inflation.
But Sniderman said there is too much uncertainty about the actual level of the NAIRU and its causal link with inflation for it to be a useful, stand alone guide of monetary policy at the moment.
"When the unemployment rate gets below 6.0 percent, it's a sign of labor market tighteness. But is that a sign of inflation? I can't tell," the Cleveland Fed economist said.
Sniderman said inflation ultimately results from overly accommodative monetary policy. But, he added, it is hard for the Fed to tell when it is being overly accommodative.

"It is always difficult to know whether current policy is resulting in inflation drifting down or creeping up," he said. "There is always a difference of opinion about that." He said it may be useful for the Fed to adopt a clear objective, such as targeting the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
Sniderman has authored a research paper on the issue of targeting CPI. New York Fed President William McDonough has defined price stability as a core CPI range between 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent.
The Cleveland Fed is hosting on Thursday and Friday a conference on the "Dynamic Effects of Monetary Policy."
The Federal Open Market Committee is next meeting on November 13. The Fed has left the 5.25-percent federal funds rate unchanged since January 31, 1996.
